CIT - TWO WORLDS COLLIDE

By: Nicky Troll | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
You’ve seen the videos, you know how know how it plays out – but not many people know what goes down leading up to those big cash-in-transit explosions. In this investigation, we’re going to

Unique Selling Point:
** UNIQUE SPIN ON TELLING CASH-IN-TRANSIT STORY
** UNDERCOVER
** INCREDIBLE ACCESS TO UNDERWORLD


Summary:
Hardly a day goes by without a bombing somewhere in the country. Cash-in-Transits are a crime of choice – delivering big bounties. Robbers know it, and work hard – planning these heists meticulously. Security Companies know the risk and invest in technology and intelligence to protect the cash they transport around the country – working around the clock to counter the constant threat of attack.

We’ve done this story before. But now, we tell it from perspective of two men essentially at war – a CIT robber planning his next heist and a CIT security guard – risking his life to deliver cash and earn a salary.

It’s a clash of two worlds.

Further information:
Cash-in-Transit criminals are not amateurs – they are at the top of criminal food chain in
South Africa. They are highly skilled and play a game of militaristically planned robberies
with high stakes in a sophisticated criminal underworld.

CIT BACKGROUND
When it comes armed robberies the biggest bounties are in CIT trucks. Millions of rand is transported on the country’s roads every day - as a largely unbanked population there is a huge demand for cash, there are around 2500 cash in transit vehicles on the road every day – each one a potential moving target ready for criminals to hit. These heavy armoured Cash-in-Transit vehicles are being blown up almost every day – with an average of 6 a week.

TREATMENT
Start with visuals of two men getting ready – both dark, both leave and drive off – one will be early sunrise, one will be late afternoon sunset. We only reveal who they are towards the end of the scenes. Script will say something about the worlds colliding – visuals of CIT explosions.

We cut to a presenter Link – we know the stats – 30% increase, 6 CIT a week, a bomb almost every day in the country. Law enforcement is involved, they have jammers, they have guns and explosives. We know the security industry fights back. But we wanted to know what it really takes and spent two days with the opposing sides…. (split screen // sliding door // type link // effect /// drone /// car driving left and right /// reverse back/// )

THE VISION
The idea for the piece is to humanize the day to day role players. I’ve made contact with a CIT informant that we will spend time with speaking about MOs and the level of planning that goes into a hit – imagine as the dark side.

Then we’d like to spend time with a CIT driver, showing him getting ready for work, getting to know the man behind the bulletproof – imagine the light side. Get them being briefed at work, getting weapons, getting ready in the car – talking through the tech in the vehicle, the fears, the risk of dying. They’ve got back up in the control rooms – we’ll speak to someone there about their tech and intelligence and what they do to try and counter the CIT attacks.


THE DARK SIDE - IT’s A SYNDICATED OPERATION
There’s a budget, there’s a shopping list and a recruitment list – you need a proper squad.

There is a whole network of players involved in each heist – everything they need, can be
bought at a price – from weapons, to explosives to intel. They hire hotel rooms for meetings
to plan their next hit, need powerful cars for speed and big money for bribes.

The robbers work interchangeably with different teams – there are the shooters, lookouts,
explosives and guards. They have even been known to cause accidents blocking security or
law enforcement from getting to the scene. The gunmen are often ex-military or MK-VETs.
The gangs know what’s at play - they have between 5 and 8 minutes on the scene of a heist
and will get the job done whether the security cooperate or not. This year alone, a number
of bystanders and guards have been shot and killed.

These criminals evolve and adapt the way they operate, finding ways to circumvent the cash
security industry’s defences – even canvassing security insiders that give away the routes
and security features of the vans. They are brave, brazen and not to be under-estimated.
Cash-in-transit heists are tertiary-level crimes that rookie criminals have no hope of pulling
off. There are different gangs, they compete and sell each other out to security companies –
compromising their competitors hits with law enforcement operations.

These elements will come through in the interview as we go – but visually we’re going to show it making calls to insiders. Going to a meeting hopefully or to buy something, I’m working on the detail with the informant on the weekend. But simple things like we’ll go buy an un-rica-ed sim, and phone, I’ll work on guns or a jammer element. We’ll talk through stolen cars. But the idea is to show some of the planning that goes into it.

UNDERCOVER ELEMENT EXPLOSIVES
The explosives used are commercial-grade ones suitable for blasting projects in mines, as well as road and dam construction.
The CIT Informant – will go source explosive with a hidden camera from a supplier at a mine in Rustenburg. He’ll show us the bomb he already bought – we’ll have the footage.

THE DANGER?
Only a fraction of the CIT robbers get caught by the authorities, and even then they more
often than not they don’t end up behind bars, but rather back on the street out on bail. One
of the criminals have told me, that the first person to get paid after a successful heist is his
attorney – he needs to know if things go wrong that he’ll get out.

For the security guards, the danger is real – every day you get into a CIT vehicle, you could
get shot or even killed. The reality is these are 2 to 3 man CIT security crews taking on gun
wielding gangs of up to 15 men – they are out manned and out gunned.

IN THIS CASE, THE COPS OFTEN ARE ROBBERS
SAPS officers, SAPS flying squad members, traffic officers, current & former members of the SA National Defence Force and private security personnel – many have been arrested for their part in CIT robberies. Our CIT guy speaks to this and has made calls to Private Security insiders infront of me – we’ll try to capture that on the day.

Complicity does not end with the police, inexperienced prosecutors dealing with these cases. They face more experienced and expensive senior advocates in court, some of whom have been hired by unscrupulous lawyers and paid with the stolen money, making them part of the CIT heist ecosystem.

Equally disturbing is that CIT heists have been romanticised in townships, with robbers living the high life and splurging money on luxury goods and vehicles, as well as lavish parties.

COLLATEAL DAMAGE
CIT robberies in South Africa have escalated to the level where they pose a threat to national security, with innocent people caught in the crossfire. Innocent people have been killed by stray bullets during CIT heists and more innocent people will be killed unless law enforcement takes decisive action - this is because perpetrators of these heists carefully evaluate the situation over time and test their precision. If they notice that law enforcement is not taking preventive measures in a particular area, they interpret this as a signal to proceed with a heist.

These robbers, who don’t hesitate to murder anyone inadvertently crossing their path, live among the public – and the public should report their activities, because it’s ultimately the public that pays the price of this scourge.


FOOTAGE
There is quite a bit of footage of cash-in-transit robberies taking place on social media and
security groups. There’s great footage of criminals blowing up safes armed with rifles and
explosives.

RECENT STATS
This year alone, there were 249 CIT Heists from Jan-Oct 2023 – that’s almost 6 every week - compared to 2022 – 30 % increase.

metadata.Summary: Hardly a day goes by without a bombing somewhere in the country. Cash-in-Transits are a crime of choice – delivering big bounties. Robbers know it, and work hard – planning these heists meticulously. Security Companies know the risk and invest in technology and intelligence to protect the cash they transport around the country – working around the clock to counter the constant threat of attack. We’ve done this story before. But now, we tell it from perspective of two men essentially at war – a CIT robber planning his next heist and a CIT security guard – risking his life to deliver cash and earn a salary. It’s a clash of two worlds.
metadata.Further information: Cash-in-Transit criminals are not amateurs – they are at the top of criminal food chain in South Africa. They are highly skilled and play a game of militaristically planned robberies with high stakes in a sophisticated criminal underworld. CIT BACKGROUND When it comes armed robberies the biggest bounties are in CIT trucks. Millions of rand is transported on the country’s roads every day - as a largely unbanked population there is a huge demand for cash, there are around 2500 cash in transit vehicles on the road every day – each one a potential moving target ready for criminals to hit. These heavy armoured Cash-in-Transit vehicles are being blown up almost every day – with an average of 6 a week. TREATMENT Start with visuals of two men getting ready – both dark, both leave and drive off – one will be early sunrise, one will be late afternoon sunset. We only reveal who they are towards the end of the scenes. Script will say something about the worlds colliding – visuals of CIT explosions. We cut to a presenter Link – we know the stats – 30% increase, 6 CIT a week, a bomb almost every day in the country. Law enforcement is involved, they have jammers, they have guns and explosives. We know the security industry fights back. But we wanted to know what it really takes and spent two days with the opposing sides…. (split screen // sliding door // type link // effect /// drone /// car driving left and right /// reverse back/// ) THE VISION The idea for the piece is to humanize the day to day role players. I’ve made contact with a CIT informant that we will spend time with speaking about MOs and the level of planning that goes into a hit – imagine as the dark side. Then we’d like to spend time with a CIT driver, showing him getting ready for work, getting to know the man behind the bulletproof – imagine the light side. Get them being briefed at work, getting weapons, getting ready in the car – talking through the tech in the vehicle, the fears, the risk of dying. They’ve got back up in the control rooms – we’ll speak to someone there about their tech and intelligence and what they do to try and counter the CIT attacks. THE DARK SIDE - IT’s A SYNDICATED OPERATION There’s a budget, there’s a shopping list and a recruitment list – you need a proper squad. There is a whole network of players involved in each heist – everything they need, can be bought at a price – from weapons, to explosives to intel. They hire hotel rooms for meetings to plan their next hit, need powerful cars for speed and big money for bribes. The robbers work interchangeably with different teams – there are the shooters, lookouts, explosives and guards. They have even been known to cause accidents blocking security or law enforcement from getting to the scene. The gunmen are often ex-military or MK-VETs. The gangs know what’s at play - they have between 5 and 8 minutes on the scene of a heist and will get the job done whether the security cooperate or not. This year alone, a number of bystanders and guards have been shot and killed. These criminals evolve and adapt the way they operate, finding ways to circumvent the cash security industry’s defences – even canvassing security insiders that give away the routes and security features of the vans. They are brave, brazen and not to be under-estimated. Cash-in-transit heists are tertiary-level crimes that rookie criminals have no hope of pulling off. There are different gangs, they compete and sell each other out to security companies – compromising their competitors hits with law enforcement operations. These elements will come through in the interview as we go – but visually we’re going to show it making calls to insiders. Going to a meeting hopefully or to buy something, I’m working on the detail with the informant on the weekend. But simple things like we’ll go buy an un-rica-ed sim, and phone, I’ll work on guns or a jammer element. We’ll talk through stolen cars. But the idea is to show some of the planning that goes into it. UNDERCOVER ELEMENT EXPLOSIVES The explosives used are commercial-grade ones suitable for blasting projects in mines, as well as road and dam construction. The CIT Informant – will go source explosive with a hidden camera from a supplier at a mine in Rustenburg. He’ll show us the bomb he already bought – we’ll have the footage. THE DANGER? Only a fraction of the CIT robbers get caught by the authorities, and even then they more often than not they don’t end up behind bars, but rather back on the street out on bail. One of the criminals have told me, that the first person to get paid after a successful heist is his attorney – he needs to know if things go wrong that he’ll get out. For the security guards, the danger is real – every day you get into a CIT vehicle, you could get shot or even killed. The reality is these are 2 to 3 man CIT security crews taking on gun wielding gangs of up to 15 men – they are out manned and out gunned. IN THIS CASE, THE COPS OFTEN ARE ROBBERS SAPS officers, SAPS flying squad members, traffic officers, current & former members of the SA National Defence Force and private security personnel – many have been arrested for their part in CIT robberies. Our CIT guy speaks to this and has made calls to Private Security insiders infront of me – we’ll try to capture that on the day. Complicity does not end with the police, inexperienced prosecutors dealing with these cases. They face more experienced and expensive senior advocates in court, some of whom have been hired by unscrupulous lawyers and paid with the stolen money, making them part of the CIT heist ecosystem. Equally disturbing is that CIT heists have been romanticised in townships, with robbers living the high life and splurging money on luxury goods and vehicles, as well as lavish parties. COLLATEAL DAMAGE CIT robberies in South Africa have escalated to the level where they pose a threat to national security, with innocent people caught in the crossfire. Innocent people have been killed by stray bullets during CIT heists and more innocent people will be killed unless law enforcement takes decisive action - this is because perpetrators of these heists carefully evaluate the situation over time and test their precision. If they notice that law enforcement is not taking preventive measures in a particular area, they interpret this as a signal to proceed with a heist. These robbers, who don’t hesitate to murder anyone inadvertently crossing their path, live among the public – and the public should report their activities, because it’s ultimately the public that pays the price of this scourge. FOOTAGE There is quite a bit of footage of cash-in-transit robberies taking place on social media and security groups. There’s great footage of criminals blowing up safes armed with rifles and explosives. RECENT STATS This year alone, there were 249 CIT Heists from Jan-Oct 2023 – that’s almost 6 every week - compared to 2022 – 30 % increase.
